result:
Everything you have ever seen arrived late.

Not metaphorically—literally. Light takes time. The sun you see in the sky is a report from eight minutes ago. The moon shows you where she was a second ago, which sounds trivial until you realize you have never once seen anything as it happens. Your own hands, reaching for a cup, are pale images transmitted at light-speed to eyes a foot away. Even the mirror lies politely, handing back a version of you fractionally out of date.

Astronomers call this lookback time. They point their telescopes like ears pressed against old letters and read galaxies as they were when the universe was young. In a sense, astronomy is just archaeology performed with better lighting.

But here's what moves me: nothing is exempt. Sound drags further behind—you see lightning before hearing it, watching the sky happen twice. A friend's voice crosses a room slower than their smile. Every conversation is really two people arriving slightly after their own beginnings.

We tend to treat delay as loss, something subtracted from the immediacy we were owed. But maybe the opposite is true. If everything arrives late, then the past isn't behind us at all—it's continuously being delivered. The world keeps showing up on time for an appointment it schedules slightly before now.

You are always meeting yesterday just as it slowly turns into today, which means every single moment of seeing is a small act of receiving mail addressed, patiently, to the present.
